paper_text:
The Effects of Electronic Cigarettes on Oral Microbiome and Metabolome in 3D Tissue-Engineered Models

Abstract
Background and aim
Recent studies have shown that electronic cigarettes (ECs) use disrupts the oral microbiome composition and diversity, impairing the metabolic pathways of the mucosal cells. However, to date, no reports have evaluated the role of EC exposure in the context of oral metabolome
Hence, the aim of this study was to investigate the role of EC aerosol exposure in the dysregulation of the oral microbiome and metabolome profile using in vitro 3D organotypic models of human oral mucosa. Methods
3D tissue-engineered human oral mucosa models were generated and infected with oral microbes obtained from saliva of a healthy donor
The epithelial surface of the oral mucosal models was exposed directly to the EC aerosol (flavoured; with and without nicotine) as it came out of a simulated activated device that mimicked the clinical situation. A comprehensive assessment of oral microbiome community composition by bacterial 16S rRNA gene sequencing was performed. A gas chromatography-based mass spectrometry analysis was also conducted to identify the effect of vaping on the oral metabolome profile
Results
A higher alpha diversity in flavoured EC with nicotine groups was observed compared to controls, with notable differences in bacterial taxa abundance. Metabolomics analysis further demonstrated distinct clustering of control, EC with flavoured nicotine, and flavoured EC groups, confirming 13 metabolites that were statistically higher in levels in flavoured EC with nicotine group, indicating the adverse effects of nicotine on the oral mucosa model

However, to date, no reports have evaluated the role of EC exposure in the context of oral metabolome. Hence, the aim of this study was to investigate the role of EC aerosol exposure in the dysregulation of the oral microbiome and metabolome profile using in vitro 3D organotypic models of human oral mucosa. Methods
3D tissue-engineered human oral mucosa models were generated and infected with oral microbes obtained from saliva of a healthy donor
Altered metabolites were mainly enriched in pathways associated with oral cancer progression. Conclusion
This study underscores the significant impact of EC use on oral health, highlighting alterations in the oral microbiome, bacterial composition, and metabolite profiles via a clinically relevant in vitro 3D organotypic model of human oral mucosa
Key words: Electronic cigarette, microbiome, metabolome profile, tissue engineering, oral mucosaIntroduction
Smoking is one of the major preventable causes of cancer. 1,2 However, awareness against the ill effects of smoking has increased due to extensive research in the field. This has led to the exploration of healthier alternatives to conventional smoking as well as better smoking cessation tools
Electronic cigarettes (ECs), or vaping as the practice is called, have received tremendous attention as a safer substitute. 3,4 The underlying assumption is that cigarette smoke has around 80 known carcinogens and ECs, deliver nicotine in a smokeless manner, thus making the latter a safer choice. 5, 6, 7 Citing these reasons, ECs have been widely used and extensively promoted as a safer smoking cessation tool as well as a safer alternative to traditional smoking
8, 9, 10
In the last decade, the popularity of flavoured ECs has increased rapidly among users, particularly among the younger generation. 11, 12, 13, 14 In 2022, 14% of high school students and 3% of middle school students were reported to use ECs. Among these EC users, 85% used flavoured ECs and most of these ECs contained nicotine. 11,15 Given that ECs have been around for about 15 years now,14 their long-term side effects are yet to be fully understood
This incomplete understanding makes this surge in EC usage, especially among the younger generation, a particular concern. It is to be noted that these flavouring agents have been deemed safe only for ingestion, and the toxic effects of inhalation of these chemicals need further investigation. 14,16
In addition to this, it is insufficiently appreciated that heating of EC liquid leads to thermal decomposition of many of its constituents resulting in release of several toxicants
17, 18, 19 The efficacy of ECs as a smoking cessation tool has also come into question. Studies have found that users, in fact, become addicted to ECs and start using them either alone or in addition to conventional smoking in the long term,20, 21, 22 hence achieving a systematic nicotine concentration that is similar to traditional cigarettes. 23 While knowledge about ECs’ adverse effects is still limited, recent evidence suggests that ECs can lead to a wide range of biological ill-effects
In vitro and in vivo studies have shown that EC usage causes inflammation,7 delayed immune response,5 oxidative stress24 cell senescence25 and DNA damage,26 hence leading to various diseased states including cancer. Oral cavity is especially significant in the context of smoking as it harbours a complex population of microbes either permanent or those destined to be housed in the respiratory or gastrointestinal tracts. Smoking is widely known to result in alterations in a healthy oral microbiome
27 Studies show that EC usage not only results in an increased susceptibility to bacterial and viral infections but also a reduced clearance of these pathogens from the body. 5,7,28,29 It has also been found to be responsible for oral microbiome dysbiosis through the promotion of an anaerobic oral environment. 30
Concurrently, the integrity of cellular metabolism is essential for maintaining cellular homeostasis and mitigation of toxic insults
31,32 However, how EC exposure associated oral microbiome dysbiosis results in the dysregulation of the oral metabolome remains under-appreciated and under-studied. There is a lack of comprehensive studies characterising the biological effects of EC aerosol exposure in oral microbiome dysregulation
To increase our understanding of the role vaping plays in oral microbiome-mediated dysregulation of oral metabolome, we performed a comprehensive assessment of oral microbiome community composition by bacterial 16S rRNA gene sequencing. A gas chromatography-based mass spectrometry analysis was also conducted to identify the effect of vaping on the oral metabolome profile
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to investigate the effect of EC aerosol (flavoured; with and without nicotine) on the health of oral mucosa at the metabolic level using in vitro 3D organotypic models of human oral mucosa while the link with oral microbiome provides an added advantage
Materials and methods
Cell culture
Human buccal squamous cell carcinoma cell line (TR146) d from Sigma-Aldrich (catalogue number 10032305-1VL) was cultured in 1:1 mixture of Dulbecco's Modified Eagle's Medium and Ham's F-12 Nutrient Mixture (DMEM:F12) (Sigma-Aldrich)
Normal human oral fibroblasts were harvested from healthy patients undergoing oral surgery with their written informed consent under appropriate ethical approval from the Mohammed Bin Rashid University Institutional Review Board (IRB). Oral fibroblasts were cultured as previously described by Moharamzadeh et al. 33 Briefly, the biopsy tissue was minced finely using a scalpel in a petri dish. The tissue was then incubated overnight with 0
05% (w/v) collagenase type I (Sigma-Aldrich, catalogue number c3867-1vl) dissolved in DMEM:F12 medium at 37 °C. To prepare the tissue for cell culture, it was carefully disaggregated by pipetting the media up and down several times. The tissue was centrifuged at 1500 rpm for 4 minutes to collect the cell pellet. A mixture of DMEM and F12 medium was used to culture the cells subsequently
TR146 and human gingival fibroblasts were cultured and expanded into monolayers to generate a sufficient number of cells for creating 3D tissue-engineered oral mucosal models. Generation of 3D oral mucosa models
The 3D oral mucosa models (OMMs) were generated as described previously by Dongari-Bagtzoglou and Kashleva34 with some modifications as mentioned below. Briefly, oral fibroblasts were trypsinised, centrifuged, and resuspended in DMEM:F12 medium to get 1 million cells per model
Each model was composed of 1 mL collagen gel populated with 1 million fibroblast cells, followed by the addition of 2 million TR146 cells. Constitution of 1 model is as follows: 10 × DMEM—110 μL; 10 × Reconstitution buffer—110 μL; FBS—150 μL; L-Glutamine (100 mM)—10 μL; Collagen (5 mg/mL)—720 μL; NaOH to set pH 7; Oral fibroblast cells—1 million. (10 × Reconstitution buffer: Hydroxyethyl piperazinyl ethane sulfonic acid (HEPES)—20 mM, sodium bicarbonate—2. 2 g, water—100 mL, NaOH—0. 062 N)
All the reagents were kept on ice, and the plasticware like falcons and pipette tips were prechilled at −20 °C before use. The reagents were thoroughly mixed with gentle pipetting to avoid generation of air bubbles. The gels containing fibroblasts were loaded into 6 well tissue culture inserts (EMD Millipore, catalogue number PIHA03050, Sigma Aldrich) and allowed to solidify for 2 hours in a 37 °C, 5% CO2 incubator
Following solidification step, the gels were completely submerged in DMEM:F12 medium and incubated for 24 hours. Then 2 million TR146 cells were seeded on gels containing fibroblasts. The models were kept in culture for up to 5 days. Infection of OMMs
The OMMs were infected with the oral microbes or microorganisms (MO) from the saliva of a healthy, nonsmoking human using a modification of a previous protocol,35 generating an oral mucosa model containing microorganisms (OMM MO)
Saliva was used to inoculate an overnight culture in LB broth at 37 °C. This culture was then used to start a secondary culture of actively dividing bacteria to infect OMMs. The suspension culture was centrifuged at 500 g at room temperature for 10 minutes. The supernatant was discarded, and pellet was washed three times with phosphate buffer saline (PBS). A Neubauer chamber was used to assess the number of microbes. The final inoculum was adjusted to a density of 107 cells/mL in PBS
For inoculation, 100 µL of this suspension was added to the OMMs. 100 µL of PBS alone was added to the uninoculated controls. The models were then incubated for 2 hours in a 37 °C, 5% CO2 incubator, which was followed by an exposure to falvored (Flv) ECs aerosol, with and without Nicotine (Nic), as described below in the coming section. The models were then further incubated for 24 hours at 37 °C, 5% CO2, after which they were again exposed to EC and incubated for a final 24 hours
Infected models that were not exposed to ECs aerosol are reffered as OMM MO NE. EC-Exposure protocol
Voopoo Drag S EC device (manufactured in China by Voopoo) was used to generate the EC aerosol. This device is rechargeable, with a replaceable heating coil and a refillable tank for e-liquid with 4. 5 mL capacity. Mint flavour e-liquid with 25 mg/mL nicotine (SaltNic Labs) and mint flavour e-liquid with 0 mg nicotine (BE LOYAL, VALUED, KIND, BLVK; USA) were used in this study
For control, the models were exposed to ambient air. The epithelial surface of the OMMs in the test groups was exposed directly to the EC aerosol as it came out of a simulated activated peristaltic pump device (Huiyu-pump; YZ15-13A). All exposure experiments were conducted under a sterile condition in a laminar flow hood equipped with a high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filter. EC puffs were given for 20 minutes with continuous puffs of 4-second duration with 30-second intervals
The pump was operated at a flow rate of 380 mL/min, which was sufficient to activate the EC and deliver aerosols through the tube into the exposure chamber. Metagenomics
Bacteria were pelleted from the culture medium of control and EC exposed OMMs at the end of the 48-hour incubation period
After DNA extraction, the V3-V4 hypervariable region of the 16S rRNA gene was PCR amplified using NEB Phusion High-Fidelity PCR Master Mix (New England Biolabs) with 16S Amplicon PCR Forward Primer = 5ʹ ACTCCTACGGGAGGCAGCAG; 16S Amplicon PCR Reverse Primer = 5ʹ GGACTACHVGGGTWTCTAAT using the following cycling parameters: 98 °C for 3 minutes, followed by 30 cycles of 98 °C for 45 seconds, 55 °C for 45 seconds, 72 °C for 30 seconds, and a final elongation step of 72 °C for 7 minutes
An Ampure XP bead (Beckman-Coulter) cleanup step was then utilised to remove the nonspecific products, which were visualised on an Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer instrument (Agilent Technologies) and quantified via the real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR; EvaGreenTM). Samples were pooled into equal molar proportions and sequenced on the DNBSeq G400 platform of MGI (Microorganism Sequencing Product Portfolio)
Negative extraction controls (sterile PBS) were included to ensure that no exogenous DNA contamination occurred during sample processing. Bioinformatics analysis workflow
Raw data was filtered to obtain the high-quality clean data, after which clean reads that can overlap with each other were merged into tags and further clustered into operational taxonomic unit (OTU). Taxonomic classifications were assigned to OTU representative sequence using the Ribosomal Database Project database
Analysis like alpha diversity, beta diversity, differential species analysis, network, and model prediction was carried out based on OTU profile table and taxonomic annotation results. Data filtering
Raw data was filtered to generate high-quality clean reads according to a previously published protocol. 1 Briefly as follows:

1. Reads whose average Phred quality values were lower than 20 over a 25 bp sliding window were truncated
Reads whose lengths were 75% of their original lengths after truncation were removed. 2. Reads with low complexity or ambiguous base (N base) and those that were contaminated by adapter sequences and ambiguous base (N base) were removed. Tags connection
In case of paired-end reads overlap with each other, a consensus sequence was generated by FLASH (Fast Length Adjustment of Short reads, v1. 2. 11). Details are as follows:

1. Minimum overlapping length: 15 bp. 2
Mismatching ratio of overlapped region: ≤ 0. 1. OTU clustering
Tags were clustered to OTU with USEARCH (v7. 0. 1090), as follows:

1. Tags were clustered into OTU with a 97% threshold by UPARSE. 2. Chimeras were filtered by UCHIME (v4. 2. 40). For 16S rDNA and ITS sequences, chimeras in OTU were screened and filtered by mapping to gold database (v20110519) and UNITE (v20140703), respectively, whereas de novo chimera screening was carried out for 18S rDNA sequences. 3
All tags are mapped to OTU representative sequences using USEARCH GLOBAL to calculate OTU abundance table. Metabolite extraction and derivatisation for secretome analysis
Quality control (QC) was created by pooling equal volume (150 µL) of conditioned media from all samples. Prior to metabolite extraction, 100 µL of QC was spiked with 0. 5 µL of internal standard ribitol (1 mg/mL). Four volumes of methanol (400 µL) were added to the spiked sample to extract the metabolites
The mix was vortexed and incubated on ice for 2 hours. After centrifugation at 10,000 g for 10 minutes the supernatant was dried in a SpeedVac. To the dried sample, 25 µL of methoxyamine hydrochloride in dry pyridine (20 mg/mL) was added. The sample was vortexed and incubated at room temperature (RT) overnight. Silylation was performed by adding 25 µL of N,O-Bis(trimethylsilyl)trifluoroacetamide (BSTFA) in 1% Trimethylchlorosilane and vortexed for 2 minutes, followed by incubation at RT for 1 hour
The derivatised sample was finally centrifuged at 10,000 g for 10 minutes and the supernatant was transferred to a glass vial insert (200 µL) in a GC vial (2 mL capacity) for gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC-MS) analysis. Similarly, various secretome QC sample sizes (10, 50 µL) were processed for further analysis along with a standard amount of ribitol (0. 5 µg)
GC-MS analysis
GC-MS analysis was performed using a GC2030 gas chromatography coupled to a QP2020 NX quadrupole mass spectrometry (Shimadzu). First, GC-MS run protocol was optimised with the QC sample. The derivatised metabolites (1 µL) were injected into a Rxi-5Sil MS column (5% diphenyl, 95% dimethylpolysiloxane; 30 m × 0. 25 mm × 0. 25 μm; Restek) in a split mode (1:5). Flow rate of the helium carrier gas was set as 1 mL/min and injection port temperature fixed at 70 °C
Both the ion source and interface temperatures were set at 300 °C. Ions in the quadruple were scanned with an event time of 0. 3 seconds between the 50 and 700 m/z range. A solvent delay of 5 minutes was used. The following 3 different GC methods were used to obtain the optimised separation method of the metabolites: GC1: 70 °C for 2 minutes, ramp of 10 °C/min to 200 °C, hold for 4 minutes, ramp of 15 °C/min to 280 °C, hold for 4 minutes (run time 28
33 minutes); GC2: 70 °C for 2 minutes, ramp of 4 °C/min to 200 °C, hold for 4 minutes, ramp of 15 °C/min to 280 °C, hold for 4 minutes (run time 47. 83 minutes); GC3: 70 °C for 2 minutes, ramp of 10 °C/min to 130 °C, hold for 1 minute, ramp of 4 °C/min to 180 °C, hold for 2 minutes, ramp of 2 °C/min to 200 °C, hold for 1 minute, ramp of 15 °C/min to 300 °C, hold for 2 minutes (run time 43. 17 minutes)
Among the different GC-MS methods, the GC3 method was used for sample volume optimisation (10, 50, and 100 µL) for the extraction of metabolites. Subsequently, 10 µL of sample was used for metabolite extraction, and GC3 method was used for metabolite separation for the remaining test samples. All test samples were randomised using an online tool (www. randomizer. org) and were run in GC-MS with one QC after every 4 samples
Data preprocessing
Firstly, the raw data obtained by GC–MS-QP2020 was integrated by GCMS solution 4. 52 software (Shimadzu). The integration conditions were set as follows: the initial peak number was kept at 5, and the slope and variable parameter time were set to 100/min and 1000/min, respectively. Next, the data obtained was registered to the NIST 11 Standard Mass Spectrometry Database (NIST) for the identification of metabolites from selected variables
Enrichment analysis
To gain insight into the metabolomic mechanisms, pathway and metabolite set enrichment analysis (MESA) were implemented using MetaboAnalyst-6. 0, an online metabolomics data analysis software. 36 Over-representation analysis (ORA) was performed using the hypergeometric test to evaluate whether a metabolite set is represented more than expected by chance within the given compound list. The concentrations of statistically significant metabolites that have p <
05 are considered for quantitative pathway enrichment analysis. Multivariate and univariate statistical analysis
The normalised data was scaled to mean-centred and divided by the standard deviation of each variable followed by multivariate analysis (MVA) using MetaboAnalyst 5. 0
36,37 First principal component analysis (PCA) was performed with all oral mucosa model (infected and non-infected) and exposed and non-exposed to ECs aerosol groups: OMM, OMM MO non exposed (NE), OMM MO Flv (Microorgranisms exposed to Flavored E-cigarette), OMM MO N+Flv (Nicotine+ Flavor), and QC to ascertain the inherent clustering pattern and outliers
Subsequently, the QC samples were removed, and partial least square discriminant analysis (PLS-DA) was performed with the remaining groups for supervised classification. To assess overfitting of the model, R2 (goodness of fit) and Q2 (goodness of prediction) values were determined using the leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) method. To further assess the reliability of the model, permutation test statistics was used with 100 permutation numbers
Univariate analysis was performed between the OMM MO NE, OMM MO Flv, and OMM MO N+Flv groups using one-way ANOVA and post-hoc Tukey's test with GraphPad Prism (8. 0. 2, GraphPad Software). All data points were plotted as mean ± standard error of the mean. Results
Sequencing output
The oral microbiome was analysed in control, flavoured EC and flavoured EC with nicotine-exposed groups in triplicates. After DNA extraction, all samples gave a 260/280 reading between 1. 8 and 2. 1
After 16S rRNA amplification and sequencing a total of 6,17,997 sequences were read, of which 6,14,112 sequences were retained after quality filtering and chimera removal. All samples were sequenced at a sequencing depth of >60,000 reads with an average number of sequences 68666 per sample and a standard deviation of 304
Alpha and beta diversity among EC-exposed and control groups
Alpha diversity was accessed using several matrices like observed OTUs, Chao index, ACE index, Shannon index, and Simpson index. Significantly higher diversity was found between control and flavoured EC with nicotine groups for observed OTUs, Chao, ACE, and Shannon indices (one-way ANOVA test, p <. 05) (Figure 1)
OTU Venn map (Figure 2A) and Core-Pan OTU plots (Figure 2B) were generated to access the common and unique OTUs between the 3 groups. Next, the beta diversity was examined using Bray Curtis Dissimilarity (Figure 2C) and weighted UniFrac (Figure 2D) indices. Both estimate the differences between communities with an abundance of information. A clear and significant clustering was observed for the 3 groups by both PCA (Figure 2E) and partial least square discriminant analysis (Figure 2F). Fig. 1

Dysregulation of oral bacterial taxonomic composition in EC and control groups
We next investigated the changes in the abundance of dominant bacterial taxa (taxa present at ≥0. 5%) between the 3 groups (Figure 3). The dysregulation of oral bacterial taxonomic composition in EC users compared to control groups revealed significant differences in the abundance of dominant bacterial taxa. The study identified notable variations (p <
05) between the control group and flavoured EC with nicotine groups across various taxonomic levels. Specifically, at the phylum level, Proteobacteria and Firmicutes exhibited alterations, while at the class level, Actinobacteria, Bacilli, Bacteroidia, and Clostridia were affected
At the family level, Prevotellaceae, Enterobacteriaceae, Bifidobacteriaceae, Ruminococcaceae, Veillonellaceae, and Lachnospiraceae, while at genus level Prevotella, Bacteroides, Bifidobacterium, and Clostridium_XlVa showed differences
Notably, taxa such as Firmicutes at the phylum level, Bacilli and Bacteroidia at the class level, Prevotellaceae and Enterobacteriaceae at the family level, and Prevotella at the genus level, were significantly impacted in flavoured EC users, irrespective of nicotine presence. Differentially abundant bacterial taxa in the salivary microbiota in control and OMMs exposed to EC-flavour or EC-flavour+ nicotine, based on 16S rRNA sequencing. Data are represented as mean ±SD. (*p <. 05, **p <. 01, ***p <. 001). Significant difference (p <. 05) determined by a one-way ANOVA with Tukey post-hoc test. Differential secretion of metabolites by cells when treated with ECs
To obtain the metabolites in the secretome, first, the GC-MS protocol was optimised
GC1 run was first used to determine the broader metabolite coverage. Several metabolites did not show optimal separation due to a steep ramp between 70 and 200 °C. Therefore, the ramps were modified accordingly in GC2 and GC3. It was observed that GC3 showed the optimal separation of metabolites with greater coverage (Figure 4). Also, among the three sample volumes used for metabolite extraction, 10 µL showed no peak saturation with maximum coverage of metabolites when separated using GC3 protocol
Subsequently, the 100 µL of test sample was used for metabolite extraction, and GC3 protocol was used for metabolomics analysis. Our optimised protocol was able to identify 93 metabolites covering amino acids, organic acids, monosaccharides and their derivatives, disaccharides, and other molecular classes (Supplementary Table S1). Upon data preprocessing and MVA, PCA results show clear clustering of the OMM, OMM MO NE, OMM MO Flv, and OMM MO N+Flv groups (Figure 5)
Interestingly, all the QC secretomes were grouped together at the intersection of PC1 and PC2 indicating that the QC is qualitatively and quantitatively representative. The entire collection of samples included in the study and all the GC-MS experimental runs in between the QCs were stable and did not lead to any significant inherent instrumental variations
In addition, as expected, metabolites secreted by the OMM model formed a distinct cluster from all the 3 OMM MO groups indicating a characteristic secretome of the OMM model in the presence of oral microbes. This distinction was further evident in PLS-DA analysis. Our results not only show clear clustering of the OMM group, but an improved separation was also observed among the OMM MO groups exposed with or without EC (Figure 4)
This indicated a significant metabolite imbalance in the secretome due to EC exposure. Since PLS-DA is prone to overfitting, the model was validated with cross-validation techniques. R2 and Q2 values of 0. 97 and 0. 63, respectively, confirm the validity and predictive ability of the supervised model. Further, a p value <. 01 obtained from the 100 permutations indicated that our model is better than the permutated models (Figure 5)
All these results indicated that the PLS-DA can predict the dysregulated secretome of the OMM upon EC exposure. In addition, we used univariate statistics to identify the dysregulated metabolites. Our one-way ANOVA results indicated that 16 metabolites were differentially altered between the control (OMM MO NE) and EC exposure (OMM MO Flv and OMM MO Flv+Nic (Micro-orgranisms exposed to Flavored E-cigarette containing Nicotine)) groups (Figure 6)
As expected, one of these metabolites included nicotine, which was found to be abundant in the nicotine exposure group. Among the other 15 metabolites, 13 showed statistically higher levels in the OMM MO Flv+Nic compared to both OMM MO NE and OMM MO Flv groups indicating the adverse effects of nicotine on the OMM. In contrast, 2 metabolites, including arabinose and threonic acid, showed lower levels in the OMM MO Flv+Nic
Interestingly, other than these 2 metabolites, no other molecule showed significant alterations upon Flv exposure alone as compared to the control. The current study conducted a comprehensive assessment of the oral microbiome community composition using bacterial 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Additionally, gas chromatography-based mass spectrometry was employed to analyse the effect of EC aerosol exposure on the oral metabolome profile utilising 3D OMM

Discussion
The impact of EC use on the oral microbiome has been a subject of growing interest and concern. Several recent studies have highlighted the association of ECs to various oral symptoms and pathologies, including dental and periodontal damage,38, 39, 40 that are linked to increased inflammatory processes,41,42 that potentially leads to a condition known as oral dysbiosis
41,43 In this study, clinically relevant, 3D tissue-engineered human OMMs were generated and infected with oral microbes obtained from saliva of a healthy donor. The epithelial surface of the oral mucosal models was exposed directly to the EC aerosol (flavoured; with and without nicotine) using a simulated activated device
The findings of this study highlight the alterations in the oral microbiome, particularly anaerobic taxons like Clostridium, Prevotella, Veillonellaceae, and Bacteroides upon EC exposure, potentially leading to metabolic imbalances. A comprehensive assessment of oral microbiome community composition by 16S rRNA gene sequencing was performed
The study specifically examined alpha diversity, and the results indicated significantly higher diversity between the control and flavoured EC with nicotine groups, which is consistent with other clinical-based studies that employed 16S rRNA gene sequencing to investigate the difference in bacterial abundance and diversity between EC users and nonusers. The results of these studies demonstrated significantly higher alpha diversity in the saliva of EC users as compared to non-EC users
42,44,45 On the other hand, the same studies have shown a higher beta diversity in buccal samples of EC users as compared to controls. 42,44 The observed bioactivity among EC users in saliva was attributed to saliva heterogenicity. 46 Interestingly, it was suggested that both E-cig and conventional smokers share similar microbiome characteristics,44 emphasising the potential risks of EC use
According to the human oral microbiome database, there are around 700 species of bacteria residing in the oral cavity, together with viruses and fungi. 47 While inter-individual differences are present, it is widely acknowledged that the overall oral microbiome is stable in the absence of any internal and external stresses that disrupt homeostasis
48 The oral microbiome of a healthy individual typically consists of Actinomyces, Capnocytophaga (gram-negative bacteria), Eikenella (genus: Neisseria and Kingella), Eubacteria (gram-positive bacteria), Fusobacterium, Haemophilus, Lactobacterium (Lactobacillus), Leptotrichia, Neisseria, Porphyromonas, Prevotella, Propionibacterium, Peptostreptococcus, Streptococcus, Staphylococcus, Veillonella, and Treponema bacterial species
49 Our data reveals significant changes in the abundance of dominant bacterial taxa on EC exposure among the three studied groups. Affected taxa that was abundant in the flavoured EC with nicotine group included anaerobic Clostridium, Prevotella, Veillonellaceae, and Bacteroides. Similar dysregulation in the levels of several of these bacterial taxons on EC usage has been reported elsewhere
For example, Prevotella, Veillonella,42,43
Bacteroidia, Bacilli, and Proteobacteria44 have been described to be significantly dysregulated in saliva of EC users as compared to control human subjects. EC usage has been reported to promote an anaerobic oral environment. 50 We believe that this EC-induced anaerobic oral environment favours the growth of anaerobic bacterial taxons thus resulting in oral microbiome dysbiosis
Of note, it has been shown that these identified taxons are mainly correlated with chronic lung diseases such as pneumonia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and asthma, including lung cancer. 51 In addition, some species, such as the Prevotella, are known to belong to microbial communities of the respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts, hence having access to airways and gastrointestinal tract via saliva swallowing
Although they may serve as commensals at these extra-oral sites, they may also potentially act as harmful agents to mucosal surfaces, leading to gastrointestinal and respiratory health and disease. 52 Such an alteration in microbial diversity and shifts in the bacterial composition by increasing pathogenic bacteria and decreasing healthy commensal bacteria may impact what is known as oral microbiome dysbiosis
Oral microbiome dysbiosis has been reported in various oral diseases like periodontitis, oral lichen planus, and Fanconi anaemia patients. 53 A study by Park et al. has demonstrated the significant increase in the effects of EC smoking mediators on gingival inflammation; these include Actinomyces, Rothia, Neisseria, and Enterococcus, leading to microbiome dysbiosis
50 In addition, a dysbiosis oral microbiome has also been shown to be a risk factor for various systemic diseases like diabetes,54 cardiovascular diseases,55 and cancer. 56 Dysbiosis in the oral microbiome, resulting from imbalances in microbial populations, can contribute to various oral health problems such as dental caries, periodontal diseases, and halitosis
45,47,57,58 Taken together, these findings align with previous studies that have highlighted the impact of EC use on the oral microbiome, emphasising the importance of understanding how ECs influence oral bacterial composition and potentially impact oral health. This, in turn, has been linked to an elevated risk of declining periodontal, dental, and gingival health, along with alterations in the oral microbiome. Case reports have detailed significant dental harm caused by EC explosions
59, 60, 61 The constituents present in EC vapor are recognised for their cytotoxic, genotoxic, and carcinogenic characteristics. 62, 63, 64
To gain an insight into the oral microbiome-associated metabolic changes due to EC exposure, mass spectrometry and metabolite enrichment analysis were employed
Data analysis revealed a total of 96 metabolites, 16 of which were differentially altered between the control group and those exposed to EC, with a notable increase in nicotine levels in the exposed group. The metabolomics analysis showed distinct clustering of the OMM and OMM groups exposed to ECs, indicating a notable metabolite imbalance due to EC exposure. The PLS-DA analysis confirmed this imbalance, with R2 and Q2 values of 0. 97 and 0
63, respectively, validating the model's predictive ability. Additionally, arabinose and threonic acid were among the metabolites with lower levels in the EC exposure group, while exposure to flavourings alone did not lead to significant alterations compared to the control group. To have a better understanding of the metabolic mechanisms by which the identified metabolites are involved, data extracted from MetaboAnalyst 5. 0 indicated that these metabolites had a major impact in different pathways
The top or highly identified pathways were mainly associated with glucose and energy metabolisms. These include methionine metabolism, homocysteine degradation, serine metabolism, and phenylalanine and tyrosine, in addition to other enriched pathways such as ketone body metabolism, glucose-alanine cycle, and Warburg effect. Interestingly, these top enriched pathways have been identified as tumour biomarkers or pathways associated with cancer progression via DNA methylation
65,66 Particularly, methionine metabolism is a gateway to oral cancer. It is documented that elevated levels of methionine by cancerous cells are referred to as the Hoffman effect. The Hoffman effect, together with the Warburg effect, contribute to the continuous growth and proliferation of cancer cells. 65 Similarly, the phenylalanine and tyrosine pathways are the main energy sources of rapidly growing cancerous cells due to their metabolic regulation of glucose and fats in the body
67,68 Of note, the homocysteine pathway is an intermediate crosslinking with the methionine pathway. This indicates the contribution of this pathway in driving oral health to a cancerous state. Various reports have highlighted homocysteine as a tumour marker in various cancers,69,70 and recently in lung and oral squamous cell carcinomas
69,71
These findings demonstrate the significant impact of EC exposure on the secretome of the OMM, contributing to our understanding of the effects of EC exposure on disrupting oral health, as previous reports have also linked the disrupted metabolism to the dysregulation of other essential cellular pathways such as fatty acids biosynthesis as well as glutathione, pyruvate, nicotinate and nicotinamide, and amino acid metabolism
72 Overall these findings highlight the potential metabolic imbalances that occur as a result of EC exposure and support previous research on the harmful effects of EC exposure on the oral microbiome and metabolite profile. 73
This study serves as a proof of principle evidence of the adverse effects of EC aerosol on oral microbial and metabolic profile. However, there are a few limitations
It remains unclear whether the dysregulation of the oral metabolome subsequently alters the oral microbiome or if the reverse is true. Furthermore, the specific molecular signalling pathways affected by EC usage, which contribute to changes in microbial and metabolomic profiles, require further elucidation. Conclusions
The microbiome has increasingly been linked to cancer
The current study underscores the significant impact of EC use on oral health, highlighting alterations in the oral microbiome, bacterial composition, and metabolite profiles. Given the importance of oral microbiome in driving cancer progression, the findings of this study emphasise the need for further investigations into the metabolic imbalances induced by EC exposure and their implications for oral health and risk to other diseases

Background and aim
Recent studies have shown that electronic cigarettes (ECs) use disrupts the oral microbiome composition and diversity, impairing the metabolic pathways of the mucosal cells. However, to date, no reports have evaluated the role of EC exposure in the context of oral metabolome
Altered metabolites were mainly enriched in pathways associated with oral cancer progression. Conclusion
This study underscores the significant impact of EC use on oral health, highlighting alterations in the oral microbiome, bacterial composition, and metabolite profiles via a clinically relevant in vitro 3D organotypic model of human oral mucosa. Key words: Electronic cigarette, microbiome, metabolome profile, tissue engineering, oral mucosa
